title: Moving backup and restore off Oracle's own tools
question: Tell me about a time you replaced a piece of working legacy infrastructure.

situation: I spent two years on a mission-critical, enterprise-scale SWIFT application used for routing international financial messages between global banking institutions. Its database backup and restore path ran on native, Oracle-specific tooling — which sat awkwardly inside an application that had to compile and behave identically across several operating systems, and which put a core piece of the data path outside the application's own control.
task: Move backup and restore off those native tools and onto a unified, application-driven migration framework, without interrupting a system handling international financial data. The codebase made that harder than the idea sounds: massive, legacy C++98, with a hybrid architecture of Java web services over a C++ core and an early, partially implemented multi-tenant model that had to be carried across carefully.
action: Migration framework: I replaced the Oracle-specific backup and restore mechanisms with a single application-driven framework, so the migration path became something the application owned and could reason about rather than something delegated to the database vendor's tooling.

Legacy refactoring: getting there meant working through highly complex legacy functions running past a thousand lines, and decoupling database logic that had accumulated in them into migration code that could be maintained on its own terms.

Around it: to get high-throughput thread safety before the modern standard libraries existed, we engineered custom thread-safe string implementations and advanced entity-component concepts; and I spearheaded code security initiatives using Coverity and runtime code guards.
result: The application's data migration path was significantly modernised and brought under the application's own control, while the system maintained 100% uptime and the compliance standards required for international financial data processing.

challenge: Navigating the sheer scale and constraints of a cross-platform C++98 codebase while bridging synchronous C++ logic with asynchronous Java web services — and doing it to a mechanism that could not be allowed to fail.
hardestBug: Less a single bug than the friction around finding them: running fully manual integration tests in a complex, multi-OS financial environment, where verifying a migration meant exercising it by hand on every platform. That bottleneck is what motivated my interest in robust automation in the roles that followed.
learned: Deepened my expertise in enterprise software security with Coverity, in memory management, and in cross-platform compilation guards — the last of which is exactly what makes a database path portable or not.
enjoyed: Decoupling complex legacy database functions into elegant, maintainable migration code, and the architectural problem-solving around it — including building the custom thread-safe components the core needed.
